title: Accolades for Team Members Not Yet Ready for Prime Time Foster Team Cohesion
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article argues that leaders who reserve praise for top performers unintentionally erode team cohesion, and that deliberately recognizing developing team members changes the whole group's culture. It contrasts results-oriented leaders who lavish attention only on stars with leaders who actively seek out contributions from those still learning the role. Concrete tactics are offered — asking reserve team members for their opinions first, or having them lead after-action debriefs — as ways to signal that everyone's contribution counts. The piece closes by tying this practice to deeper relational payoffs: stronger cohesion, checked egos among top performers, and a team identity built on mutual investment rather than a star system.
points: The core claim is that a team's culture is set less by how it treats its stars than by how it treats those not yet contributing at the top level.
Practical tactics — asking developing team members for their opinions first, or having them run after-action debriefs — operationalize the philosophy rather than leaving it abstract.
The essay identifies a specific failure mode of results-oriented leadership: praise concentrated only on top performers breeds envy and a fractured team ethic.
It links recognition practices directly to checking the egos of star performers, not just to boosting morale among reserves.
quotes: There is no such thing as an insignificant team member on a highly cohesive team. The team wins or loses as a unit, not as a collection of stars and reserves.
Too often, results-oriented leaders and coaches give attention, time, and accolades exclusively to their top performers.
The best leaders and coaches look for reasons to recognize and acknowledge those behind the “starting” unit.
Leaders who frequently give accolades to those “riding the bench” foster a different team mentality than do others.
This places a check on the egos of those on the stage and reminds them that they succeed when everyone else on the team does as well.
